content.p: On 2 November 1920, the day Americans chose Warren Harding over James Cox for president, a Black farmer named Mose Norman tried to vote in the Florida citrus town of Ocoee and was turned away. By the next morning a white mob had hanged and shot his friend July Perry, burned the northern Black neighborhood and put the survivors to flight. The Orange County Regional History Center calls it the largest incident of voting-day violence in United States history.

Nobody has established how many Black residents died. Contemporary newspapers spoke of fewer than ten dead, two of them white. Later estimates go as high as 60. No one was ever charged. For decades, according to the Orlando Sentinel, public officials and the press called it a "race riot", a label that often implied the Black community had caused it.
content.h2: A town built on citrus and labor
content.p: Ocoee grew from a labor camp of the 1850s beside Starke Lake, near Lake Apopka. By 1920 it was an unincorporated settlement; it did not become a city until 1925. Florida's state audit office, OPPAGA, counted 255 Black and 560 white residents in the 1920 census, and noted that the 1910 count had been 225 Black and 304 white. Most Black families lived in one of two clusters, the Northern or Methodist Quarters and the Southern or Baptist Quarters, each named for its church.

Perry and Norman had both come from South Carolina in the late nineteenth century. Perry, a deacon and a labor boss through whom white growers hired Black pickers, was in his fifties in 1920. Ages differ by source: the Orlando Sentinel gave 50, the Florida History Blog 51. Norman worked a 100-acre family orange grove and was among the first people in Ocoee to own a car. Both held leadership roles in the local fraternal lodge. Perry's great-niece, Sha'Ron Cooley McWhite, told the Sentinel that he "was lynched not because he had done anything wrong, but because he had done everything right."
content.h2: The 1920 campaign and the Klan's warnings
content.p: It was the first presidential election after the 19th Amendment gave women the vote. Republican politicians in the South were working with Black leaders to register voters, who leaned Republican. OPPAGA reported that the Ku Klux Klan staged marches in Jacksonville and Orlando to frighten Black residents before the vote. The Klan's Florida leader wrote to Orlando attorney William O'Neal, threatening him for going "among the negroes" and explaining how to become citizens; a copy went to John Cheney, a local attorney and former judge who was a Republican candidate. Cheney said the Ocoee Klan had told him there would be "serious trouble" if Black residents tried to vote.

According to the Florida History Blog, the Klan paraded through both Black neighborhoods of Ocoee on the night of 1 November with megaphones, warning that no Black person would be allowed to vote. Florida also taxed the ballot: Fox 35 reported that Florida was one of four states relying on the poll tax to impede Black voting. Accounts disagree on the amount. Fresh Take Florida put it at $2, mentalfloss.com at $1.

Poll workers told Norman he could not vote because he had not paid his poll tax. Some accounts say he had paid it; the museum notes that sources conflict. He went to Orlando and saw Cheney, who, according to OPPAGA, advised him to go back and write down the names of anyone refused and of the officials refusing them. He returned and was turned away again.

What happened next is told two ways. In one version, the local constable found a shotgun in Norman's car, took it, and sent him on his way. In the other, a group of white men searched the car, found the gun under a seat, and beat Norman when he came back to it; he escaped on foot. Both versions agree that he went to Perry's home and then left Ocoee the same day. The Florida History Blog adds that he reportedly shouted "We will vote, by God!" at the poll workers, but that is not in the state report.
Norman had already left. According to the Florida History Blog, he visited friends near Apopka on 3 and 4 November, then moved to New York City, where he lived until his death in 1949.

Later that day a group of white residents formed a posse, deputized by Orange County deputy Clyde Pounds, to arrest Perry and Norman. It was led by Sam Salisbury, a former army colonel and former chief of police in Orlando. Perry was at home with his wife Estelle and his daughter Caretha, who appears as Coretha in some sources.

The attempt to arrest him ended in gunfire. OPPAGA records that several posse members were wounded, Salisbury among them, and that two, Leo Borgard and Elmer McDaniels, were killed. Perry and Caretha were also wounded. Details of how it started are contested. The Florida History Blog says Salisbury took hold of Perry and Caretha raised a rifle, which went off; The Guardian, summarising Ortiz's research, says Perry himself fired a shotgun at the crowd and killed two men. The state report does not say who fired the fatal shots.

The posse pulled back and called for help from Orlando and elsewhere in the county. During the pause Perry and his wife left the house. When Sheriff Frank Gordon and more men arrived, they seized Caretha inside the house and captured Perry in a sugarcane patch near his house. He was taken to a hospital in Orlando for his gunshot wounds.

OPPAGA says only that Perry, in the sheriff's custody after leaving the hospital, was taken by a white mob, hanged and shot. Other accounts give more, and they conflict. The Florida History Blog and The Weekly Challenger say he was taken from the Orange County jail, with the sheriff handing over the keys, then dragged behind a car to the area near Cheney's home and hanged. The Guardian, citing Ortiz, says he was pulled from the jail by Klansmen. The Florida History Blog and The Guardian both report that a note or sign was left at the scene saying, in language that used a slur, that this was what happened to Black people who voted. The Fresh Take Florida account places the hanging near Country Club Drive and says it may have been an oak tree; the blog describes a telephone pole along the highway.

Estelle and Caretha Perry were taken by deputies to the county jail in Tampa, reportedly for their own safety. Perry's death certificate, the Orlando Sentinel noted, gave the cause as "by being hung not by violence caused by racial disturbance." The Florida History Blog says a Black undertaker, Edward Stone, cut the body down against the Klan's wishes and buried it in Orlando's Greenwood Cemetery, where the grave remained unmarked until a headstone was added in 2002.

With Perry in custody, a mob burned the buildings of the northern Black neighborhood through the night, as late as 4:45 on the morning of 3 November, OPPAGA found. The count of what was lost varies slightly: the state report says more than 20 houses, two churches (Ocoee African Methodist Episcopal and Friendship Baptist) and the Ocoee Lodge 66 hall; historians quoted by the Sentinel say 25 homes, two churches and a lodge. The Florida History Blog says a school was also burned and that people who ran from burning buildings were shot. It also relays the recollection of a 93-year-old former Klan member about eight people burned in a house. The state report does not confirm these details.

Ex-servicemen's groups from Orlando and nearby towns set up patrols in the days afterward. OPPAGA says the remaining Black residents faced threats and violence in the following months and left their homes and property. Survivors' memories carry much of what is known. Armstrong Hightower, who was 13, told of running through the orange groves with his sister and looking back at a town in flames. Allen Franks, 18, led five siblings hand in hand through swampy woods while carrying a sixth, disabled brother on his back, his daughter Gladys Franks Bell told the Sentinel. John and Roxie Williams escaped by horse and buggy, with the lighter-skinned Roxie sitting in the back so that, in the dark, a stranger might take her for white, their grandson recalled.

The toll is the least settled fact. OPPAGA reports a range from 3 killed, Perry among them, to close to 60. Two Orlando clergymen, Rev. J. A. Long and Rev. H. K. Hill, said they had heard of 35 deaths. The state report also notes that five new graves were dug in the Black cemetery in the days afterward, and that an undertaker's memorandum from the night of 2 November recorded three people burned to death in a house and buried in one grave. An NAACP inquiry, Al Jazeera reported, produced estimates of 30 to 60, according to interviews with townspeople. Records uncovered from the period point to six deaths including Perry's, the Sentinel reported in 2020. The History Center, working from land records, census data and oral histories, says it can confirm four.

Pam Schwartz, the History Center's chief curator, said documents were deliberately not kept. "There's also an intentional obfuscation of this information," she told Fresh Take Florida. She said researchers have found no photographs of the burned neighborhood.

The violence was reported in newspapers across the United States and Canada, OPPAGA found. The NAACP sent a representative, Walter White, who arrived in Florida on 5 November and, posing as a buyer of orange groves, interviewed people in Ocoee and Orlando. He drew on that work in congressional testimony on 29 and 30 December 1920, before the House Census Committee. The National Equal Rights League asked the US Attorney General to look into Perry's lynching.

The Justice Department assigned the task to Herbert Phillips, a Florida district attorney, who took the question to be only whether federal election laws were broken. His report said there had been "no attempt to intimidate any Negroes in the casting of their ballots." An Orange County grand jury, convened by Judge Charles Andrews, found "no evidence against any one or group of individuals as to who perpetrated the fatalities". The same grand jury cleared Estelle and Caretha Perry of charges linked to the deaths of Borgard and McDaniels, and they were released from the Tampa jail on 30 November 1920.

Within two weeks, advertisements offering groves in Ocoee for sale appeared in Orlando and Miami newspapers, OPPAGA reported. The state report says it is hard to tell whether Black owners were paid, or paid fairly. Perry's estate was placed under the administration of Bluford Sims, a local citrus pioneer. Three years later Perry's family petitioned the court to recover it, claiming they had not been compensated. When the court ordered an accounting from Sims's guardian, Eva Sims, none was filed, and the court did nothing further after the February 1924 deadline. A restriction written into the deed barred conveying the property "to a negro". The Florida History Blog gives one example of a sale price: Hightower received only $10 for a 37-acre tract, it says.

The intimidation continued. In July 1921, the Orlando Sentinel reported that 15 men took George Betsy, a former Ocoee resident, from two police officers; he was found chained to a light pole because, a report said, he had "talked too much about the trouble at Ocoee." Five men were arrested that summer for dynamiting and shooting into a Black family's home near Ocoee; two, William Moore and Frank Saunders, were found guilty in September 1921.

The census tells the rest. OPPAGA estimated that at least 253 Black residents were displaced; the 1930 count showed two Black residents among 1,180 white. The state report says Black residents did not return to live in Ocoee until the 1970s; the Florida History Blog gives 1978, and a James Madison University history of racial-terror markers gives the 1980s. Ocoee remained a "sundown city", in the Guardian's phrase, with census returns showing only white residents from the massacre until 1980.

For decades the story survived mostly in family memory. A research group called the Democracy Forum spent about two years in the 1990s working through census records, property records and death certificates, and presented its findings to the city of Ocoee in 1998, according to Fresh Take Florida. In 2010 the historian Paul Ortiz published an essay calling the day "the single bloodiest day in modern American political history."

The city's response came in stages. Ocoee created a human-relations advisory board in 2006, the James Madison University project notes. A marker reading "Hallowed Ground" was erected in 2018 by the mayor and a local reconciliation task force. In November 2018 the city commission adopted a proclamation declaring Ocoee a "sunrise city". In April 2018 the Equal Justice Initiative included the events in its National Memorial for Peace and Justice in Montgomery, Alabama. On 21 June 2019 Orange County unveiled a marker for Perry at Heritage Square in Orlando, with the EJI's Bryan Stevenson speaking at a ceremony. The city also issued a formal apology, which the University of Central Florida's oral-history project lists among its government documents; the Orlando Sentinel described a letter of apology to be offered to descendants in October 2020.

OPPAGA's review, published in November 2019, was carried out as directed by the Legislature. In 2020 Senator Randolph Bracy and Representative Kamia Brown, both Democrats, pushed for compensation for descendants like that paid at Rosewood, but did not win support in the Republican-controlled Legislature; Fresh Take Florida reported that the Senate bill passed unanimously but was unlikely to clear the House before the session ended. Instead, lawmakers unanimously passed House Bill 1213, which requires the massacre to be taught to Florida students; the governor, Ron DeSantis, signed it on 23 June 2020. The 2021 Legislature created the Randolph Bracy Ocoee Scholarship Program for up to 50 students who are direct descendants of victims or current Black residents of Ocoee, worth up to $6,100 a year.

On 2 November 2020, the centennial, DeSantis proclaimed 1920 Ocoee Election Day Massacre Remembrance Day after a request from the American Civil Liberties Union of Florida and the Orange County NAACP. The branch's president, Beverlye Colson Neal, called the text "watered down" because it left out language from the groups' draft about statewide harm and modern voter intimidation, but said she was glad of the recognition. The Orange County Regional History Center opened its exhibition, "Yesterday, This Was Home: The Ocoee Massacre of 1920", that autumn.
